item.title: Now, We Should Be Doubly Concerned About Whom We Interact With
item.description:
Microbiome

Now, We Should Be Doubly Concerned About Whom We Interact With

How social groups shape our microbiome and may influence our behaviors and thoughts.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Social interactions shape our beliefs, identity, and personality.
  • Close social relationships can promote microbial sharing beyond immediate family members.
  • Our microbiome may influence our mood, cognition, personality, and social behavior.

In any group we are in, whether it is family, friends, or a workplace, we gradually share each other's customs, beliefs, and types of thoughts. This happens so smoothly and gradually that we rarely notice it; yet, it can profoundly shape the deepest layers of our identity. Our social interactions play a crucial role in shaping our identity and self-concept. The feedback we receive from those around us can either boost our self-confidence or lead to feelings of dissatisfaction and constant comparison with others. We may even modify or suppress some aspects of ourselves to conform to group norms. According to social identity theory and self-categorization theory, we largely define ourselves through our membership in groups. Many people derive their sense of importance from the groups to which they belong. These groups tell us “who we are” and “how we should behave.”

However, these influences are not one-way; we also impact the networks of which we are members. By joining a group, we change its dynamics. Our thoughts, behaviors, and even lifestyles, in turn, affect other members depending on our position within the group's hierarchy. It is a dialectical relationship: We create networks, and networks create us.

Professional networks also determine our success in career development: who we collaborate with, who notices our work, and who invites us to opportunities. Over time, small advantages in your network grow into big differences in visibility and opportunity. The good news: Because success depends on networks, we can change those networks to make things fairer.[1]

Study of Microbial Sharing in Close Social Relationships

However, social interactions influence some hidden aspects of us that are hard to believe. A recent Nature study mapped both the social networks and gut microbiome of 1,787 adults living in 18 remote villages in Honduras. Using strain-level genomic analysis, the researchers found that close social relationships were associated with extensive microbial sharing, not only among family members but also among friends and neighbors, even after accounting for factors such as diet, medications, and household environment. Remarkably, the study revealed that microbial similarity extended beyond direct relationships to friends of friends, suggesting that our microbiome may be shaped by the broader social network in which we live. This article clearly showed that social networks can shape a biological feature of their members, microbial composition, alongside their established effects on social behavior and identity. [2].

Although this article did not address the transfer of other microbial populations, such as those inhabiting the mouth and vagina through social contact, it is plausible that the oral and vaginal microbiomes could be transferred more easily within closed populations. Additionally, the authors did not discuss the physical and mental health consequences of this microbial uniformity in such populations. However, it is well recognized that our microbiome significantly influences the function of our body’s organs.

These observations raise a fascinating question: To what extent do social groups directly influence the beliefs, thoughts, and decisions of their members, and to what extent might these effects result from the microbes they transfer to one another?

The Role of the Microbiome in Cognition

Interest in the role of the microbiome in cognition has led to extensive research in this area. Although most studies have been conducted on animal models, human evidence strongly suggests that the cognitive effect of this microbial population on the mind is remarkable. The trillions of microbes living in your intestines talk to your brain constantly through a two-way highway called the gut-brain axis. Your gut is not just digesting food; it is quietly running a side operation that influences how you think, feel, and act. They act in the brain through common ascending neurons that signal to the brain, and through modulation of immune and endocrine axes, and also some chemical compounds. Serotonin, dopamine, GABA, and short-chain fatty acids: Your gut microbes help produce and regulate these mood-shaping molecules.[3] So, when your microbiome is out of balance, your emotional baseline shifts as well.

But it goes deeper. Some studies suggest that certain microbial profiles correlate with personality traits like desires, extroversion, or anxiety-proneness. Others have linked gut health to decision-making under risk and even social behavior. Ever felt a "gut feeling" about something? There might be actual biology behind that intuition.

Your gut microbes may be quietly co-authoring your personality. Emerging research links microbial diversity to sociability, anxiety traits, and even the strength of our identification with social groups, mediated through inflammation, chemical compounds, and neurotransmitter signaling. It is a strange thought: the self we call "identity" might partly be negotiated with trillions of nonhuman cells residing within us.[4]

Overall, it is well established that the microbiome influences our desires, emotions, thoughts, and personality. Therefore, it is logical to conclude that some aspects of social influence on us may be mediated through microbial transmission. The self you call “you” may not be entirely your own. Some of your traits, desires, and even beliefs might be co-authored by microbes you picked up from the people you chose to spend time with. This is in addition to the well-known effects of microbial transmission on health. So, the next time you find yourself repeatedly spending time with a certain group and notice a gradual shift in your mood or desires, ask yourself: Was it their words, or their microbes?

item.title: Love and Grief: How the Body Remembers
item.description:
Grief

Love and Grief: How the Body Remembers

Personal Perspective: The physicality of grieving my dog Holly.

Posted August 10, 2026

My husband Jim and I took our dog Holly to the veterinarian last week and came home carrying only her collar. It still had the little metal tag on it.

Holly Rowe

Holly Rowe
Source: Used with permission/Maggie Rowe

I hadn't realized how much of loving a dog is physical until there was no longer a body there. I miss Holly burrowing against my side in the middle of the night. I miss coming home to the frantic scratch, scratch, scratch of her paws as she hurried to greet me. I miss the particular texture of her tongue and those tiny determined licks that made my husband and me joke she ought to have a "licker license." More than anything, I miss the way she altered the pace of my days. Holly's energy was never hurried. When you were with her, you naturally slowed down. You lingered a little longer. Her rhythm quietly became your rhythm, and without realizing it, your own nervous system began to match hers.

Until she was gone, I hadn't understood how much of love lives not in our thoughts but in our bodies.

When the Body Grieves

Kacheve Stafford
Source: Kacheve Stafford, used with permission

Recently, on 50 Words for Snow, the podcast where my co-host Emily Garcés and I explore words that have no direct English equivalent, we spoke with Kacheve Stafford, who grew up in Trinidad and Tobago. He introduced us to the Trinidadian word tabanca. As he described it, tabanca is the profound ache that follows separation from someone you love. What struck me wasn't simply the definition but the way he talked about it. He described people losing weight because they couldn't eat, becoming physically diminished after a loss. Even when Trinidadians jokingly talk about having a "curry tabanca" because their favorite curry shop is closed, the joke works because everyone recognizes the same underlying truth: Longing is something the body experiences, not just the mind.

That conversation gave me a different way to understand my own grief. I don't just miss Holly emotionally. I miss all the places where her body used to meet mine. My hand still reaches automatically to the empty space beside me on the couch. I still pause after the gate closes, expecting to hear the joyful scramble of her feet racing toward me. My body continues performing a choreography that no longer has a partner. For a fraction of a second each day, it remembers before my mind catches up.

What Love Leaves Behind

Emily ended that episode with a beautiful poem imagining an ancient castle feeling tabanca for the life it once contained and a kestrel mourning the trees that once filled an open field. The poem suggested that perhaps places remember, too. That perhaps longing is woven into the fabric of the living world.

I've been thinking about that ever since. About how our house remembers Holly. The hallway remembers the sound of her paws. The space beside me in bed remembers the curve of her little body. Even the quiet moments of the day seem to remember when she would have wandered into the room, asking for dinner, asking to go outside, or simply reminding me, by her unhurried presence, that there was nowhere more important to be than exactly where we already were.

Maybe that's why words like tabanca matter. They don't lessen grief, and they don't explain it away. They simply give dignity to an experience that can otherwise feel lonely and inexpressible. They remind us that love leaves traces. It changes the way we move through a day, the speed at which we walk, the places our hands instinctively reach, the sounds we expect to hear. Long after the one we loved is gone, those small bodily habits remain, quietly carrying the shape of that love.

item.title: Why Stay Together After an Affair?
item.description:
Relationships

Why Stay Together After an Affair?

To repair or to retaliate after an affair?

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Extended retaliation after an affair may be unproductive, even harmful.
  • Reparative behaviors give the relationship a chance to heal.
  • Many couples stay together after an affair.

The Pew Research Center reported that 90 percent of Americans consider an extramarital affair to be morally wrong (Evans & Corichi, 2026). Yet, according to data from the U.S. General Social Survey (GSS), 16 percent of married people surveyed had at least one affair (Davern et al., 2022). The Institute for Family Studies found that 75 percent of the men in their study had a larger number of sexual and sexual/emotional-combined affairs, while 56 percent of the women respondents had emotional-only affairs (Dew, 2024).

Repair

Despite the painful and often traumatic side effects of an affair, a recent study found that 75.5 percent of those who had been unfaithful ended their affairs and reconciled; 79 percent of those cheated on remained with the partner who had been unfaithful (Nickerson et al., 2026). These couples preferred to salvage their relationships to preserve the integrity of their families, please parents and grandparents, or spare children the stress of divorce. Some also stayed for cultural and religious reasons, or because they were in love. Many faithful partners who choose to stay do so for reparative reasons—that is, to give the relationship a chance to survive and thrive. A reparative commitment is evident both in and out of treatment by a sincere desire and effort to improve the relationship.

Retaliate

There are, however, retaliative reasons that faithful partners choose to stay in a post-affair relationship. And these individuals do so at the risk of bringing the relationship into a nihilistic, sadomasochistic cycle. For example, a faithful partner may become obsessed with the affair and repeatedly bring it to the transgressing partner’s attention for an “extended” time—maybe even years after the transgression. While the unfaithful transgressor must tolerate a certain level of anger from his or her faithful partner, if the deluge drags on without any new insight, especially on the part of the faithful partner, the post-affair relationship may begin to reflect the cause of the affair.

The partner cheated on may also insist on bringing up the transgression at certain events such as a family wedding, public event, or even in an intimate setting. Such maneuvers are designed to inflict humiliation or evoke shame. During sex with his wife, a husband suddenly stopped the lovemaking and angrily asked if his sexual ability compared favorably to that of her ex-lover.

Not all retaliative behaviors are conscious or easy to identify; many are in fact passive. For example, a faithful partner may withhold sex from an unfaithful partner. While this can be a symptom of posttraumatic depression, it may also reflect an underlying aggression or rage toward the unfaithful partner. A woman I treated admitted she consciously stopped making her adulterous husband breakfast or supervising his medication routine. Another man chose to respond to his wife’s affair by curtailing her freedom. He admitted that he did not fear another affair as much as he felt his wife merited a “grounding” for her transgression and so he chose to punish her as he would one of the couple’s unruly children.

I have found that faithful partners who cannot let go of an affair may have experienced a form of infidelity in past relationships or experienced adultery in their families of origin (e.g., father cheating on mother). Others may have narcissistic qualities (e.g., “No one cheats on me”). Regardless, a pre-existing internal rage might have already been in place and awaiting detonation.

Unfaithful transgressors who stay for a good beating may have sufficient guilt and feel they deserve it. Certainly, they must take responsibility for their adulterous behavior and learn a new and effective way to communicate their relational unhappiness. If, however, they, too, are not sincere in their desire to better the relationship, and this includes setting appropriate limits with the amount of punishment they absorb, they might eventually act out again.

Summary

No doubt, in certain contexts, the impact of an affair might suddenly unveil a posttraumatic response from a faithful partner. A movie or song may do the same. But again, how long these reactions persist, whether the faithful partner can consider the entire system that produced the affair, and whether he or she is sincerely interested in getting the help needed to manage the trauma are crucial in distinguishing a reparative from retaliatory reasons to stay in a relationship. Although not the focus of this article, the unfaithful transgressor must learn to communicate his or her dissatisfaction with the relationship. He or she should also gain access to any residual internalized feelings that may have contributed to or be behind the transgression to avoid acting out again.

item.title: What 8 Weeks Without Social Media Taught Me
item.description:
Media

What 8 Weeks Without Social Media Taught Me

Personal Perspective: What surprised me most about from stepping away from the online world.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • We don’t need to capture every beautiful moment to fully experience it.
  • Stepping away from social media can bring us closer to the people we care about.
  • When fewer things compete for our attention, there is more room for our own lives.
Source: Photo by Glen Carrie on Unsplash

I’m eight weeks into my summer experiment of being off social media, and I’m loving it. At this point, I have absolutely no desire to go back.

And yet, I probably will at some point. I’m an author, after all. I have readers I love to chat to online, books I want to share, and the occasional thought I’d like to put out into the world. There’s also a little voice in my head saying, "But shouldn’t you be on there?" Maybe I should. Maybe I shouldn't. Thankfully, I don’t have to decide today.

For now, I’m enjoying this little experiment and paying attention to what has happened in the space social media left behind. When I wrote the first part of my summer experiment, I was mostly curious about how to stop scrolling. Eight weeks in, I’m more interested in what has taken its place.

So far, there have been three things I didn’t expect.

1. Social media can make us feel connected without actually connecting us.

When I first deleted my social media apps, I missed seeing updates from my favourite writers, horse trainers, and various interesting people I had accumulated in my online world. And then I realised something: I didn’t actually know most of these people.

Meanwhile, having lived in seven countries, I have friends all over the world. Although I already see my local friends regularly, I realised I could be much more proactive about staying connected with the ones who live further away. Without social media giving me the feeling that I was “keeping up” with everyone, I started actually keeping up with the people I care about.

I sent more messages. I organised calls. I had long conversations with friends I hadn’t properly spoken to in far too long. I found myself rekindling friendships that had never disappeared, but had perhaps been sitting on the sidelines of busy life. I wonder whether that is one of the strange things social media does: gives us the feeling of connection without necessarily giving us the connection itself.

Research supports the idea that stepping away can make a difference. A 2022 study found that people who took a one-week break from social media experienced improvements in well-being, depression, and anxiety.

Perhaps it isn’t simply about how connected we are, but about how connected we actually feel. There’s a big difference between seeing someone's holiday photo online and actually hearing their voice when you ask how they really are.

2. There is a little withdrawal, but it passes.

The first few weeks off social media brought two slightly embarrassing habits to my attention. The first was occasionally thinking, "Oh, this would make a nice picture to post." The second was wondering what some of the random people I followed were up to. Both bothered me for slightly different reasons.

I realised I don’t want to experience my life through the imaginary eyes of an audience. I don’t want to see a beautiful sunset and immediately think about how it would look in a story. I want to see the sunset. Sure, I still take photographs. I love capturing memories. But there is something wonderfully different about taking a picture because you want to remember something and taking one because you want other people to see it.

To overcome this, I simply started practising noticing. A beautiful view? Notice it. A lovely smell? Notice it. Something funny? Notice it. I don’t need to do anything with it. I can just let it be mine.

The second habit disappeared more easily. Once I stopped checking social media, I stopped thinking about what these random people were up to. And that was that.

There’s nothing wrong with following people who inspire you or being curious about other people’s lives. But it made me laugh when I thought about how strange this habit would sound if we could explain it to someone from 15 years ago: "I’m going to spend part of every day following strangers on the internet and keeping up with what they’re doing with their lives."

They might reasonably ask: Why? Honestly, I’m not sure I know anymore.

3. My attention feels different.

At first, I tried to replace social media with other forms of digital nonsense. I read the news. I checked the weather repeatedly. I browsed things I had no intention of buying. Apparently, my brain was perfectly happy to find another rabbit hole. Eventually, I caught myself doing it and managed to stop it. And that’s when I noticed my attention change.

I could sit down with a book and stay with it. I could work on something without feeling the pull to check something else. My mind wandered a lot less, and I felt less compelled to follow every little thought that wandered past. Interestingly, a 2025 study found that blocking mobile internet on smartphones for two weeks improved participants’ sustained attention, mental health, and well-being.

Of course, I’m not claiming that going off social media has magically transformed my attention span. But I do think something happens when fewer things are constantly asking for our attention. There is simply less to check, less to consume, and less to follow. And therefore, perhaps, a little more room to notice what is already here.

I have one more month left of my experiment, although I’m beginning to suspect that one month may turn into two or three. Maybe I’ll eventually return to social media, but with a completely different relationship to it. Maybe I’ll find a way to use it for my work without allowing it to become part of the background noise of my everyday life. I don’t know yet. And, strangely, I’m OK not knowing.

For now, I’m enjoying fewer people to keep up with, fewer things to check, fewer moments to share, and, somehow, more of my own life to live. I’ll let you know what happens next.

item.title: In the Era of BookTok, I Went to Book Club
item.description:
Social Media

In the Era of BookTok, I Went to Book Club

Can the rise of online reading communities replace the real thing?

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • BookTok is a subculture of the social media platform TikTok that has attracted many young readers.
  • Online literature communities have helped to popularize new books and give new life to old classics.
  • Literary discourse on social media mimics the communities of book clubs but fails to foster connection.
Source: Image by Katamaheen from Pixabay

Putting my car in park, I take a deep breath before turning off my car and getting out. Although I consider myself extroverted, it still gives me pause knowing I am meeting a dozen new faces at once, and I silently rehearse introducing myself a few times as I grab my belongings out of the passenger seat.

I feel like I’m about to start the first day of high school. In reality, I’m just going to a new book club for the first time.

Despite our modern world being clothed in the suffocating swathe of social media, reading is as trendy as ever. How has reading a novel stayed a relevant hobby when the younger generations have never known a world without endless internet access at their fingertips?

The reign of BookTok–a metaphorical corner of TikTok in which content creators, celebrities, influencers, and regular people alike congregate to share opinions and recommendations of books–has carved out an invigorated new generation of readers. The impact of these online communities can be seen in any bookstore, as now many young readers gravitate to the store shelves that tout titles “as seen on BookTok” rather than the stacks of books marked with the seal of approval from various celebrity book clubs or those announcing bestseller statuses. Meanwhile, apps like Libby have provided libraries with a virtual facelift, allowing readers to buy titles or check out digital book copies using their library cards. Many young readers have also taken to apps such as Goodreads to seek reading recommendations or share their own opinions on popular titles after finishing them in the reviews section of the platform.

Resources like these have helped the timeless hobby of reading remain relevant amidst the onslaught of technology that has surged into society in recent decades. Although they have encouraged many young readers to read via online platforms, physical books are far from out-of-style. Library attendance has steadily increased since the sharp decline brought on by the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Many young readers are also trekking to bookstores or placing online orders to purchase physical copies of books for their own at-home library. “Book-fluencers”–social media influencers whose content is based on creating a reading-based aesthetic–have popularized buying physical editions of books in order to romanticise the experience of reading via book personalization with colorful pens, personalized bookmarks, and notated margins.

Has social media ruined yet another corner of our lives by turning a simple hobby into a contest to make it appear aesthetic or palatable for the general public? It may feel like it, but arguably, digital communities like BookTok and Bookstagram may just be reinventing the wheel in a way that is actually ensuring reading's survivability. The bookfluencers who share posts such as “what I read this week,” “what my Libby shelf looks like right now,” and “ten books that I think about daily” are filling the same role as the celebrity recommendations of years past, except with more (arguably performative) candidness and authenticity, thanks to the self-employed nature of many of these influencer positions. Below any given Bookfluencer’s newest post, their followers are often in lively debate, sharing opinions, recommendations, or vitriolic criticisms of the books discussed in the post.

There is no ignoring it: BookTok is yet another example of how social media can feel like an echo chamber or void. The sheer volume of opinions from every direction can be overwhelming and the interpretations of classics circulated can be enough to make a seasoned literary critic pull their hair out with frustration at the lack of reading comprehension. However, BookTok can also be credited for reinvigorating many forgotten classics and hidden gems. One such example is the 1995 novel I Who Have Never Known Men by Jacqueline Harpman, which has now sold over 800,000 copies in North America thanks, in part, to its recent rediscovery by creators online. Beyond the second life BookTok is giving many titles, the online resurgence in reading is doing something many English teachers and exasperated parents have pined for for years: making reading cool.

Moreso, the creation of virtual reading spaces has also given young people a space to conduct online conversations about books, and to create virtual guerilla book clubs. Although they are often not explicitly called book clubs, the online discourse that prevails in the comment sections of book-related social media posts is reminiscent of lively book-club chatter: praise for character development, outrage over rushed endings, and disagreements over interpretations of vague dialogue. Young people are continuing to dissect literature in a new online space, continuing conversations over old classics and paving discussions on popular new work.

Source: Image by nini kvaratskhelia from Pixabay

There is still something hollow about sharing opinions in an online space, devoid of the intimacy, camaraderie, and hors d'oeuvres of in-person clubs. Some people reply to a post with a comment only to receive no responses on their thoughtful literary critique. Others may share an innocent yet unpopular interpretation of the book in question, only to receive an onslaught of criticism from individuals they will never meet. The most popular opinions are often simply the most controversial. So, conversations over literature are happening, but there is a dissonance to them that cannot be resolved unless the conversations are continued offline. BookTok has encouraged reading and literary discourse, but cannot replace human connection. It can, however, serve as the springboard that encourages youth to read, discuss, learn, and opine.

As I sit in the circle at book club, introductions having been made and conversation about the month’s title in full swing, I look around and am struck by how glad I am that I chose to attend despite the discomfort that comes with being the newest addition to a pre-established social group.

Online reading spaces do much of the heavy lifting when it comes to encouraging the next generation to catch the reading bug, but they cannot replace the connection of discussing plot points and critiques with a group of people who can make eye contact as they listen to each other’s thoughts. I leave book club that night with new perspectives to consider, a few new book recommendations, and a dozen new familiar faces to call friends. We decide on next month’s book before parting ways, and they ask if I plan to join again for the next gathering. I say yes.

item.title: Will Sports Prepare Me for Life?
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Will Sports Prepare Me for Life?

Character developed in sports may not impact life outside of sports.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Similarity of situation impacts virtue translation across contexts.
  • Not all virtues are equally likely to translate across contexts.
  • Reflection can aid virtue development across contexts.

In 2022, Barack Obama spoke to Harvard University’s basketball team. He described how playing basketball shaped him and prepared him for leadership. “There is something extraordinary about hitching your wagon to something bigger than yourself,” he stated. He added, “The odds of any of you being LeBron or Steph, as good as you are, are not as high as the odds of you being extraordinary leaders in health care or business or civil rights.”[1]

Obama attested to the formative value of sports for character. Additionally, while it is statistically unlikely that many collegiate athletes will play at the professional level, Obama shared that their sporting experiences would prepare them for leadership in other domains.

Can Sports Form Character?

The sentiments Obama shared are common, and they may be apt. In many cases, sports can play a formative role in our character. This is for a few reasons. Sports involve practice, or intentional repetition of certain virtue-tracking actions. For example, a footballer may learn fitting fear concerning risks. A runner may learn to persevere over extended runs. A curler may learn patience, in discerning the right moment to release a stone. Accordingly, sports provide repeated opportunities to act well, in ways that are conducive to virtue development.[2]

Sports also provide opportunities to reckon with infelicities of various sorts, such as injuries, losses, and hardships. They offer practice managing heightened emotions. Sports also facilitate encounters with excellent others, such as a teammate who far exceeds another. In such cases, athletes may respond with envy. Alternatively, they can learn to respond productively to the successes of others, such as through emulation or gratitude. Sports can also provide community, affording participants the chance to connect over “something bigger than yourself,” in Obama’s phrasing. Sports do have the potential, albeit sometimes unmet, to form participants for good.

How This Process Goes Awry

Even so, there are a few reasons why sports participation will not necessarily yield improved character. First, most coaches are not prepared to coach to this end.[3] Sports performance tactics and safety training are widely mandated for school-based coaches, but only 8 percent of states in the United States mandate training in character development and sportsmanship.[4] Also, it is possible to play sports and practice vices, instead of virtues. An example is teammates who consistently envy each other, or a player who is imprudent regarding training.

Another possibility is that the character formed in sports will remain in sports, without impacting life outside of it. For example, a runner may grow in perseverance as she accumulates mileage across a season. Should we be confident that the perseverant runner will then be able to persevere as a citizen or a student? Perhaps not. This worry is called the problem of virtue translation.[5] For the remainder of this article, I will focus on this concern.

The Problem of Virtue Translation

Virtues are often situation-restricted traits. They are stable properties but are highly context-dependent.[6] For example, I may be reliably patient while gardening—reacting to slower-than-desired progress toward a goal with a reasonable level of calmness[7]—yet not exhibit virtuous patience in line at the grocery store or while interacting with my children. We often act in predictable yet fragmented ways toward the good.[8]

On these grounds, we might wonder whether the virtues acquired in sports will impact character outside of sports at all. Maybe the patience acquired while playing tennis will only affect my comportment on the tennis court. Perhaps the courage I develop on the football field will not appreciably impact my dispositions toward risk off of it. When virtues fail to translate situations, character development initiatives in sport offer minimal benefit to our lives. So, what factors impact whether virtues translate across contexts? Here are three.

1. Similarity of Situation

In Plato’s Republic, Socrates describes the value of gymnastics alongside poetry for forming guardians in his City in Speech. He does not raise a concern about virtue translation. Why? Plato wrote in a milieu marked by political conflict, where preparation for citizenship largely meant preparation for war. These are similar contexts. Forming a person’s character through sports may translate readily between physical training and the military, more so than between sports and a career in finance, for example.

Something to keep in mind is that situation-types can be cast in numerous ways, and not all of them are physical. For example, if I learn to be patient with teammates in basketball and I view my work colleagues as teammates, my patience may translate readily across contexts.

2. The Virtue in Question

Situational constraints impact certain virtues more than others. For example, resilience is a virtue that enables its possessor to cope with or overcome adversity.[9] There is considerable empirical evidence that resilience translates across contexts, which is what we might expect for a virtue defined, in part, by one’s ability to reckon productively with change and unanticipated setbacks (i.e., undesirable situational changes). Otherwise, this virtue would only reckon well with expected outcomes, which is quite unresilient. Other virtues, such as fortitude and perseverance, appear to translate less readily across contexts.

3. The Process of Development

The virtue developmental process in sport will also impact translation. For example, if practice of a virtue (e.g., perseverance) is accompanied by reflection on one’s greater life purpose and values, participants may view character growth as connected to other areas of life, like relationships, religious identity, or vocation. Absent reflection, a sports participant may habituate virtue-tracking actions but lack motivational continuity across contexts.

[1] Golen, J. 2022. Obama tells Harvard team, basketball was about more than me. KARK.

[2] Little, S. 2024. The Examined Run. Oxford University Press.

[3] Coakley, J. 2015.

[4] Atkinson et al 2022: 3; Bates & Anderson-Butcher 2023

[5] Little, S. 2026. The problem of virtue translation from sports. Theory and Research in Education 24(2): 188–208.

[6] See Hursthouse 1999; Snow 2010; Upton 2009.

[7] Miller & Furr 2025

[8] Miller 2023, 2024; Upton 2009; Kamtekar 2004

[9] Snow 2019: 126

item.title: The Dangerous Conscience of the Psychopath
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

The Dangerous Conscience of the Psychopath

Psychopaths conceal a lack of conscience and don't care what they do is wrong.

Posted August 10, 2026

According to pioneering psychopathy researcher Dr. Robert D. Hare, “Some psychoanalytic theories depict the psychopath as an individual whose antisocial behavior is ego-syntonic—that is, is an integral part of his personality and not accompanied by moral apprehension, anxiety, and guilt—and therefore not personally disturbing.”1 In other words, there appears to be a disturbance in conscience such that there is no evidence of moral emotions (shame, guilt), though there may be understanding of right from wrong.

Source: Floryn Radu/Pixabay

Fundamental disregard of others’ rights and feelings

At the 6th Biennial Meeting of the Society for the Scientific Study of Psychopathy (“SSSP”) in 2015, Lucy Foulkes, currently a psychologist at the University of Oxford, shared findings that uncovered atypical social behavior for persons with psychopathic propensities that reflected a fundamental disregard for other people’s rights and feelings. Specifically, she highlighted that “Individuals with high levels of psychopathic traits are more likely to find being cruel enjoyable and not enjoy being kind.”2

“No moral brakes!”

In a presentation at the 2026 SSSP conference in Dallas, Texas, Dr. Craig Neumann, Regents Professor from the University of North Texas and an internationally recognized psychopathy researcher, provided findings based on justice-involved adolescents and adults who were assessed for psychopathy and capacity to recognize basic moral foundations reflecting harm and fairness toward others. These data were backed up by neuroimaging carried out with the adolescents while viewing instances of moral transgressions. His conclusions provide critical insight into the dangerous nature of conscience of the psychopath. Taken together, the findings demonstrated that “the psychopath knows, both at the psychological and neurobiological level, about morals but does not care about them.”3 In other words, according to Professor Neumann, "While the person with psychopathic propensities has the capacity to recognize moral transgressions—i.e., right from wrong—they don’t report any moral emotions, and far worse, have absolutely no remorse for moral transgressions (e.g., harming another person). This makes the psychopathic person highly dangerous, because while they fully recognize when harm could be done to another person, they have no moral brakes, so to speak, and are perfectly willing to carry on with harming another person.”4

Personal experiences in the family setting

As a person who lived with a mother and sister who displayed high levels of psychopathic traits, I can validate that they knew exactly what they were doing but did not care about the consequences. I can recall telephone conversations that my mother would have with friends and family who were having difficulty with family relations. My mother, who always desired to be the center of attention, would tell the listener at the other end of the telephone just what was needed to patch a relationship and put it back on the right path. Her advice was full of understanding and assistance to ensure a peaceful ending. At hearing how well she spoke, I was amazed by these conversations. She knew what should be done, was happy to tell others what to do, but never applied these principles. Instead, at home, the consequences she created and enjoyed were turmoil, controversy, lies, and bad feelings.

My mother, who was quick to give advice to others about "the right thing to do," chose not to come to the hospital to see her newborn grandson. Instead, she shunned the event and rationalized her decision by fabricating stories and giving a labyrinth of reasons why she refused to come. Since the baby was low birthweight, there was great concern that he was all right. But I knew that when I was most vulnerable, my mother threw the most darts. My mother spoiled every moment, especially when joy was anticipated. After my mother-in-law called my mother to suggest she come to see the new baby, she arrived with my father. I was fraught with worry. As I started to cry because of fear that the baby was all right, I looked up to see a smirk on my mother’s face and thrill in her eyes. In the words of Dr. Foulkes, she enjoyed being cruel, not kind.

Psychopaths use concealment to disguise their lack of conscience

If conscience can guide us to do the right thing, as my mother knew to do with her advice, why would she do the wrong thing and inflict emotional pain on her daughter? And if a person has a dangerous conscience and accepts this, why would this person conceal what she/he does? According to Dr. Neumann, the answer is, “Because they can recognize moral transgressions, and they know others do too, their lack of conscience (‘absence of guilt’) must be disguised, else they would be cast out of social groups as pariahs never to be trusted.”5

My sister created aliases to conceal her wrongdoings using different marital names, scrambling letters and initials while changing her date of birth, making herself one year younger to cover her whereabouts so that she would not be found out. She also changed her Social Security number. Her fabricated stories were endless, depending on who she wanted to target. When she targeted someone, her goal was to destroy and her energy was relentless.

From when I was in grammar school, our religious instructor taught that a conscience was a guidepost to want to do good and keep us on the straight and narrow path, but the rational mind can intervene, distort and corrupt. According to Dr. Hare in his book, Without Conscience, “Unlike psychotic individuals, psychopaths are rational and aware of what they are doing and why. Their behavior is the result of choice, freely exercised."6

item.title: Why Unfriending People May Be Bad for Your Creativity
item.description:
Creativity

Why Unfriending People May Be Bad for Your Creativity

The people who challenge your thinking may be the ones who keep it creative.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • There is an important difference between toxicity and disagreement.
  • Unfriending reasonable dissenters helps build the very echo chambers we complain about.
  • Creative thinking depends on constructive conflict.
  • The goal isn't to change their mind. It's to keep developing yours.
Social Media Logos
Source: Adobe Stock

The Unfriend Button

You went apple picking last weekend and posted a few photos. An old high school friend comments that you should be careful. Those apples are probably covered with pesticides and genetically engineered anyway. “Frankenfood,” he calls them, another example of corporations tampering with nature.

You haven't seen him in 30 years. You remember him as perfectly reasonable. Still, you don't feel like arguing about apples. You hide his posts for 30 days.

A month later, he's back. This time it's something about electric cars. You roll your eyes and keep scrolling.

Then one morning you're already in a bad mood. He posts something else you find completely wrong. You start typing a response. Delete it. Try again. Finally, you think, Why am I doing this to myself?

You click Unfriend.

It feels good.

To be clear, I'm not talking about people who are abusive, prejudiced, threatening, or trying to sell you something. I'm talking about something much more ordinary: people whose ideas annoy you. Unfriending them may be good for your emotional health. But it may be bad for your creativity.

We Are Building Our Own Echo Chambers

We hear a lot about echo chambers, usually as something being done to us. Facebook, LinkedIn, and other platforms learn what we like, then give us more of it. Before long, the algorithm has surrounded us with people who see the world pretty much the way we do.

But that's only half the story.

We help.

Every time we hide, mute, unfollow, or unfriend someone because we disagree with them, we make our world a little more agreeable. We also make it a little narrower. Eventually, our ideas mostly encounter other ideas like themselves. We begin having what amounts to a conversation with ourselves.

Cass Sunstein, in #Republic, warns about precisely this problem. A healthy society depends partly on “unchosen” encounters, exposure to people and ideas we would not necessarily select for ourselves. Research by Eytan Bakshy, Solomon Messing, and Lada Adamic involving millions of Facebook users reached a similarly uncomfortable conclusion: algorithms influence the range of ideas we encounter, but so do our own choices.

We like to blame the algorithm for the echo chamber. But sometimes the algorithm is simply taking our instructions.

Believing in free expression is easy when we agree with what's being expressed. The harder test is what we do with reasonable ideas we dislike. We don't have to tolerate abuse, hatred, or harassment. Ordinary disagreement is different.

When we remove the loyal opposition, our ideas no longer have to defend themselves. And that's where the creative problem begins.

Creativity Needs the Loyal Opposition

The British have a wonderful political phrase: the loyal opposition. The loyal opposition isn't someone who politely agrees with you. It's someone who disagrees with you vigorously without becoming your enemy. We could use a few more of them in our social media feeds.

Creativity has never depended on everyone getting along—quite the opposite. New ideas often emerge when competing ideas collide. One position encounters another. Both are challenged. Something unexpected emerges between them: a hybrid, a third way, a possibility neither side could see on its own.

Psychologist Charlan Nemeth has spent decades studying the creative power of dissent. In In Defense of Troublemakers, she shows that exposure to minority viewpoints can stimulate divergent thinking. The important point is that dissent doesn't make us consider the dissenter's argument. It can cause us to search more widely for possibilities.

Consider that annoying high school friend again. Maybe this time he's arguing about artificial intelligence, remote work, or whether college is still worth the money. His argument probably won't persuade you, and yours probably won't persuade him. But in trying to explain your position, you discover an assumption you can't quite defend. He qualifies one of his claims. You both see an exception. Perhaps somewhere between your positions is an idea neither of you had considered.

That's how new ideas are made. Idea meets opposing idea. Both get knocked around a little. Sometimes what survives is better than either one.

Constructive conflict isn't the enemy of creativity. It is one of its engines.

The problem with an echo chamber isn't necessarily that the ideas inside it are wrong. It's that they become intellectually soft. They don't have to withstand criticism, accommodate contradictory evidence, or evolve.

When we unfriend the loyal opposition, we don't just lose their ideas. We lose the friction that forces us to improve our own.

Don't Try to Change Their Mind

Here's where most of us go wrong. We enter disagreement trying to win.

We assemble facts. We find the perfect statistic. We send the article that will finally make the other person say, I hadn't thought of it that way. You're right.

Good luck with that.

Hugo Mercier and Dan Sperber, in The Enigma of Reason, argue that human reasoning is deeply social. We don't simply weigh facts like impartial judges. We reason with and against other people, defending positions, evaluating arguments, and interpreting evidence through what we already believe.

Perhaps we're asking the wrong question. Instead of asking, How can I change this person's mind? Ask, What might this encounter reveal about mine?

Facts alone may not change either person's mind. But the experience of wrestling constructively with someone who sees the world differently can. You begin to see where your argument is weak, where theirs is stronger than you expected, and where both of you may be missing something.

Sometimes you even discover that the other person has a point. And occasionally, they discover that you do.

Before reaching for Unfriend, try three things.

  • Know the difference between disagreement and dysfunction. Abuse, prejudice, harassment, and exploitation don't deserve your attention. Ordinary disagreement might.
  • Get curious before getting combative. Ask one genuine question: What leads you to see it that way?
  • Try changing your mind before trying to change theirs. Use disagreement to test, stretch, and refine your own thinking.

You don't need to change your old high school friend's mind about Frankenfood. You need to make sure yours is still capable of changing.

Before You Click Unfriend

Sometimes clicking Unfriend is exactly the right thing to do. Emotional boundaries matter.

But before removing someone simply because their ideas annoy us, consider what else we might be removing. Not just their opinions, but one of the forces capable of changing our own. The next time your old high school friend posts something ridiculous about Frankenfood, resist the urge to make him disappear.

You don't have to agree with him.

You might just need him to disagree with you.

item.title: How to Stop Fixing a Relationship That's Not Working
item.description:
Relationships

How to Stop Fixing a Relationship That's Not Working

If we want things to change, we have to stop rushing to "keep the peace."

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • From the time we're born, women are taught that our job is to take care of other people.
  • When our partner is angry, women's first response is usually to try to restore the bond no matter what.
  • The first step is to resist the urge to immediately make your partner OK when conflict arises.

Before I describe what I believe is the most important shift we can make when dealing with a partner’s defensiveness and anger, I want to remind us of the strong conditioning we receive as women in our culture—what we’ve been taught to believe and, thus, the soil within which this shift must grow and be trusted.

From the time we're born, women are taught that our job is to take care of other people; our value and worth rest on our capacity to be helpful, selfless, and kind—in short, to make other people happy. We’re raised to feel responsible for everyone else’s okayness, and guilty if we can’t meet others' wants and needs. At the same time, we’re taught to be peacemakers and empaths, to smooth choppy relational waters, and keep everyone pleased.

This conditioning plays a strong part in why women respond to a partner’s anger the way we do. When our partner refuses to “hear” us, to empathize with the pain they’ve caused us, when they blame us for our experience, and emotionally attack us for “aggressing” them with our pain, our first instinct, often, is to (immediately) make everything OK, “win them back,” and, essentially, convince our partner that he should still love us—we won’t be “bad” again, won’t accuse him of doing something that wasn’t OK—for us. Our first response is usually to try to restore the bond no matter what, get things back to OK, no matter what the cost to ourselves. And so we bury our pain, abandon ourselves—our focus narrows and becomes singular: to scrub all conflict from the relational space.

The Role of Survival Instincts in Relationship Conflict

But underneath this behavior is profound fear, deeply wired into our nervous system. When we launch into “fawning” behavior, making things nice (when they're not nice), we’re operating from our deepest instinct—the survival instinct—and therefore must approach this tendency and all attempts to change it with great compassion. There’s nothing light or, to some degree, optional about our need to restore the bond in situations when a partner is angry at us, even if their anger is irrational. Regardless of what we know intellectually, and whether we even like our partner or want to be with them, still, we kick into a kind of emergency gear in conflict: the front brain is entirely bypassed, and we’ll do whatever it takes to get the relationship back on track. We’ll deal with higher-level concerns like self-empowerment and authenticity when things are smooth again. Because, right now, we’ve got to take care of our most basic need: survival. The fact is, many women equate conflict in their primary relationship with death.

The root of this unhelpful (to ourselves) response lies in our fundamental conditioning as women: We’ve been taught that the way to be loved, to matter and belong, is to be liked, wanted, and pleasing. And that if we don’t belong, we're not safe and will be left behind by the herd—to die. Anything that disturbs the security of the connection—an unwanted truth, conflict, or negative experience—threatens our fundamental ground. It is not an exaggeration to say that the prospect of someone important not liking us, being displeased with us, even temporarily, stirs a kind of primal terror.

Throughout history, on a practical level, women also needed their partner to survive. The demands of pregnancy and child-rearing, and the limited educational and professional possibilities, made it impossible for women to be safe unless someone chose them and continued to choose them. We just recently achieved the opportunity and freedom to support ourselves and exist independently from a partner’s financial support.

While this situation of dependency and powerlessness may no longer be true, our generational nervous system has not caught up with our new reality. We still fear for our basic survival should our partner’s love be withdrawn.

Women are also profoundly attuned to the emotional weather in relationships in a way that’s different from men. Our brains are wired to detect any potential disruptions in harmony, no matter how minute; we’re always attending to the state of the bond. In fact, it’s hard for many women to be “OK” when the relationship is not “OK”; inner peace relies on relational peace.

Simultaneously, because women have traditionally been in charge of taking care of the children and home, the emotional well-being and stability of the family is something to which we’re highly attuned. Keeping the family environment harmonious is our responsibility, and we worry deeply about the consequences that relational conflict might cause to our children.

Numerous other factors make conflict and specifically anger in our relationships feel so threatening and trigger a response of “fawning” in whatever form it takes. At the root, however, is a primal fear: If the relationship is in danger, we’re not safe and will die. Whether it makes “sense” to the intellectual mind, which it often doesn’t, the body is still acting from that fear.

How to Begin Breaking the Habit of "Winning Him Back"

With this as our starting place, breaking our habit to “win him back” can feel scary and ridiculously hard. Still, it changes us and frees us from the enabling and unhealthy behavior that keeps us stuck, disconnected from ourselves, and deeply unsatisfied. The first step on the path to freedom is simply (but not easily) to resist the urge to immediately make your partner OK when conflict arises. It is to stop trying to fix his discomfort or unhappiness, to literally and figuratively sit on your hands and close your mouth. There is such a thing as healthy conflict—sometimes conflict has to be allowed in the relationship to move the dial forward and make things better, to change what isn’t working. If your partner’s done something to upset you, it’s OK to bring it into the light and let it sit out there, unfixed and without a follow-up apology. It’s OK and, in fact, necessary to refrain from rushing in to take away the bad feelings your truth might bring up in him.

By immediately making things “nice” again, smoothing the waters and reassuring him with your words and behavior that all is well in the relationship and with you, that you’re not upset with him, even though he hurt you, shouted at you, withheld empathy and treated you unkindly, you’re effectively removing any need for responsibility on his part. At the same time, you’re protecting him from having to see and feel the wound he opened in you. And most importantly, you’re anesthetizing any need or incentive for him to change his behavior in the future. Without meaning to, you’re communicating that he can keep doing what he’s doing—you’re fine and, in fact, are even more committed to him. There are no consequences—he’s free to continue behaving (and hurting you) in the same way.

In the next part of this series, I’ll bring some examples of what it looks like to allow healthy conflict to stand, to catch your impulse to immediately reset the apple cart that he knocked over—ultimately, to transform your behavior when it comes to this instinct to keep yourself safe by “making it work” and restoring “peace” at all costs. This process is no small affair and requires an emotional warrior’s strength—we know how to make things OK, and we're good at it, but not making things OK is new; it feels scary and unnatural, counterintuitive at every level. It’s not how we naturally roll as women. And yet, it “works” in the long run; it will change your relationship—and you.
